  1                   CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF JAMES W. DANIEL

 2                                    I.      INTRODUCTION


 3   Q.    PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME.

 4   A.    My name is James W. Daniel.


 5   Q.    ARE YOU THE SAME JAMES W. DANIEL THAT PREVIOUSLY FILED DIRECT

 6         TESTIMONY IN THIS DOCKET ON BEHALF OF THEON RANCHES, LP, AND

 7         DANIEL AND KATHRYN VOSS (COLLECTIVELY, “THEON-VOSS”) AND D &

 8         M DAVIS LAND AND CATTLE, LP (“D&M DAVIS”)?

 9   A.    Yes.


10   Q.    IN YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY DID YOU SUPPORT ONCOR/LCRA TSC’S

11         RECOMMENDED ROUTE 894?

12   A.    Yes.


13   Q.    DID    YOU     RECOMMEND           ALTERNATIVE         ROUTES      OR     LINKS       TO

14         ONCOR/LCRA TSC’S PROPOSED ROUTE 894?

15   A.    Yes. If the Commission does not approve Route 894, then I recommend that routes that

16         include Links B3, F42 and F43 not be approved.


17   Q.    WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

18   A.    I have reviewed the direct testimony of certain intervenors. My cross-rebuttal testimony

19         will address intervenor testimony related to (1) opposing the Applicants’ recommended

20         Route 894, and (2) supporting other routes or links.




     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                   Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                           1                        James W. Daniel
  1   Q.     ARE THESE THE ONLY ISSUES YOU HAVE WITH THE DIRECT TESTIMONY

 2          FILED BY INTERVENORS IN THIS CASE?

 3   A.     No. However, based on my experience with other transmission line CCN cases, and

 4          perhaps with all cases I have been involved in, this case has far more intervenor

 5          participation through direct testimony or Statements of Position than most other PUC cases.

 6          Given the procedural schedule it would take a great effort to review all the intervenor

 7          testimony and Statements of Position that have been filed and, fortunately, I was not tasked

 8          with doing that. My review was limited to direct testimony that impacted my clients’

 9          properties and filed generally by consultants on behalf of landowners versus landowners

10          testifying on their own behalf. My silence on other issues and other witnesses’ testimony

11          should not be interpreted as my agreement on those issues and with other testimony.


12    II.    CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF CERTAIN INTERVENORS OPPOSING

13                          THE APPLICANTS’ RECOMMENDED ROUTE 894

14   Q.     WERE THERE MANY INTERVENORS THAT FILED TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT

15          OF THE APPLICANTS’ RECOMMENDED ROUTE 894?

16   A.     Yes. The intervenor consultant witnesses that I am aware of that filed direct testimony in

17          support of Route 894 are provided in the Table 1 below:




     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                      Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                            2                          James W. Daniel
 1

2




    SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349       Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
    PUC Docket No. 59475          3             James W. Daniel
  1   Q.    DID ANY INTERVENORS FILE DIRECT TESTIMONY OPPOSING ROUTE 894?

 2   A.    Yes. Of the filed intervenor testimony, I focused on those intervenors that had retained a

 3         consultant as a witness that opposed Route 894. Those witnesses were: Mark Turnbough

 4         on behalf of Wulff Bluff Creek Ranch and Abell Ranches, Rae Lynn Schneider Reinecke

 5         on behalf of the Segment K13/K51 Landowners, and Thomas Ghidossi on behalf of the G-

 6         9 and G-13 Landowners. While not consultant witnesses, I will also comment on the direct

 7         testimony filed by Burnet County Commissioners.


 8   Q.    PLEASE DESCRIBE THE TESTIMONY OF WITNESS MARK TURNBOUGH,

 9         PH.D.

10   A.    Dr. Turnbough opposes the Applicants’ proposed best meets Route 894 mostly because that

11         route does not use an existing compatible ROW to cross the Colorado River. Instead, he

12         recommends alternative Route 392 which uses an existing transmission line ROW to cross

13         the Colorado River.


14   Q.    ARE THESE THE ONLY TWO ALTERNATIVE LINKS THAT CROSS THE

15         COLORADO RIVER?

16   A.    No. The Applicants proposed six links that cross the Colorado River. These are Links J11,

17         J22, J26, J31, U2 and U3. Of the 122 alternative routes considered in Oncor’s Routing

18         Memo analysis, 12 routes include Link U3, which is the link that utilizes the existing

19         transmission line ROW to cross the Colorado River.




     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                    Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                          4                          James W. Daniel
  1   Q.    DO YOU AGREE WITH WITNESS TURNBOUGH’S RECOMMENDATION FOR

 2         ROUTE 392?

 3   A.    I continue to support the Applicants’ recommended Route 894. However, I do not oppose

 4         alternative Route 392.


 5   Q.    PLEASE DESCRIBE THE TESTIMONY OF WITNESS RAE LYNN SCHNEIDER

 6         REINECKE.

 7   A.    Ms. Reinecke mostly opposes the Applicants’ proposed best meets Route 894 because of

 8         environmental factor concerns. Using the Applicants’ proposed links, she then developed

 9         a modified route that she claims reduces her environmental factor concerns from Route

10         894. Her revised route is called Cherokee Creek G (or “Route CCG”).


11   Q.    DO YOU AGREE WITH MS. REINECKE'S RECOMMENDATION FOR ROUTE

12         CCG?

13   A.    No. I disagree with Ms. Reinecke’s recommended alternative Route CCG. Ms. Reinecke’s

14         analysis prioritizes environmental factors and seemingly places less value on a route’s

15         estimated cost, length, and habitable structures. As discussed in my direct testimony, these

16         are 3 of the 4 more important factors typically used by the Commission when approving a

17         transmission line route. For the fourth important factor, the total length of a route parallel

18         to existing compatible rights-of-way (ROW), her proposed route CCG has a longer length

19         parallel to existing compatible ROWs than the Applicants’ recommended Route 894.

20         However, that would be somewhat expected since Route CCG is longer too.


21         In addition, I disagree with Ms. Reinecke’s reliance on certain additional and somewhat

22         duplicative environmental routing factors, and public meeting surveys and input.


     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                      Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                            5                          James W. Daniel
 1    Q.    PLEASE PROVIDE AN EXAMPLE OF THE ADDITIONAL ROUTING FACTORS

2          AND DUPLICATIVE ROUTING FACTORS.

3    A.    Most of the routing factors Ms. Reinecke presents to support her new route “CCG” are

4          environmental, land use and community value concerns. On pages 89 through 90 of her

 5         direct testimony, Ms. Reinecke lists 22 routing factors that she claims support her proposed

 6         Route CCG. Most of those 22 routing criteria are not included in the Commission’s list of

 7         routing criteria and are not on the list of routing criteria that the Applicants’ environmental

 8         experts considered in their Environmental Assessment and Routing Study Report (EA)

 9         submitted in the Application.


10         An example of additional routing factors Ms. Reinecke suggests supporting her route CCG

11         are those related to parks and recreation areas. The Commission’s standard application

12         form for new transmission lines requires Applicants to list all parks and recreation areas

13         within 1,000 feet of the center line of the route ROW.


14         The EA also considered the length of the route through parks and recreation areas. The

15         Applicants provided that information in their EA and includes the number of parks and

16         length through parks identified in the link and route data used for their routing study.


17         By comparison, Ms. Reinecke applies five different factors for parks and recreation areas.

18         These are: (1) the number of parks and recreation areas within 5 miles of the route, (2) the

19         acreage of parks and recreation areas between 0.5 and 1 miles of the route, (3) the acreage

20         of parks and recreation areas between 1 and 2 miles of the route, (4) the acreage of parks

21         and recreation areas between 2 miles and 5 miles, and (5) cumulative acres.




     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                       Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                            6                           James W. Daniel
  1         In my opinion, Ms. Reinecke’s introduction of these new factors over-emphasizes factors

 2         related to parks and recreation areas and skews the results in selecting a best-meets route.

 3         For example, Ms. Reinecke proposes extending the distance that a line may be near a park

 4         from 1,000 feet (the distance required by the Commission), to 5 miles. Neither Route 894

 5         nor Route CCG have any parks or recreation areas within 1,000 feet of the route. When the

 6         distance is extended to 5 miles from the route, Route 894 has 24 areas while Route CCG

 7         has 11 areas.


 8         An example of duplicative routing factors Ms. Reinecke presents relates to potential

 9         impacts on endangered species. The EA analysis includes one factor for the length of a link

10         or a route across known habitat of federally listed endangered or threatened species. Ms.

11         Reinecke’s analysis lists six factors related to endangered species and critical habitat. While

12         not downplaying the importance of the impact of a transmission line on endangered

13         species, listing six somewhat related factors as opposed to one factor exaggerates the

14         potential impacts on endangered species habitat.


15   Q.    PLEASE EXPLAIN THE PROBLEM WITH MS. REINECKE’S RELIANCE ON

16         PUBLIC       MEETING         SURVEYS          AND    FEEDBACK          TO     DETERMINE

17         COMMUNITY VALUES.

18   A.    In her direct testimony, Ms. Reinecke spends 19 pages describing how she sorted and

19         categorized responses to three questions in the public meeting surveys to determine

20         community values in the study area. In my opinion, this information is of little value in

21         routing transmission lines and in determining the alternative route that best meets the

22         Commission’s routing criteria.       Also, at the time of the three public meetings, the

23         Applicants presented their initially selected routes for the study area. After the public

     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                       Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                            7                           James W. Daniel
  1         meetings and in response to comments received, the Applicants revised some links and

2          routes and added or deleted other links or routes. These changes in links and routes

3          compared to what was presented at the public meetings are discussed in Section 6 of the

4          EA. Given the extent of these changes, one would expect the survey responses to be

 5         different if the Applicants held another round of public meetings to present the revised links

 6         and routes. The public meeting survey information Ms. Reinecke relied upon is likely

 7         outdated, so relying on that information may result in flawed conclusions.


 8   Q.    PLEASE EXPLAIN HOW THE APPLICANTS DETERMINED THE BEST MEETS

 9         ROUTE, ROUTE 894.

10   A.   Per the Application, the EA developed the statistical data for 1,246 alternative routes in the

11         study area using 171 proposed links. An Oncor routing expert, Casey Petty, then conducted

12         a routing analysis and culled 1,124 of the 1,246 alternative routes leaving 122 routes for

13         inclusion in the Application (the 1st cut).


14         Then, based on the Applicants’ response to Hodge-Schwertner RFI No. 1-17, it appears

15         that the Applicants further considered the routing data and culled another 92 routes of the

16         122 routes included in the Application leaving their Top 30 alternative routes (the 2nd cut).


17         Next, per the route analysis workbook provided in response to RFI No. 1-17, the Applicants

18         further considered the routing data and culled another 24 routes from the Top 30 routes

19         leaving their Top 6 alternative routes (the 3rd cut).


20         Finally, the Applicants further considered the routing data and selected Route 894 as their

21         best meets alternative route (the 4th cut).



     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                      Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                8                      James W. Daniel
  1   Q.    HAVE YOU COMPARED MS. REINECKE’S PROPOSED ALTERNATIVE

 2         ROUTE CCG TO THE APPLICANTS’ ROUTE CULLING STAGES?

 3   A.    Yes. I compared Route CCG with the Applicants’ Top 30 and Top 6 alternative routes.

 4         Based on that comparison, Route CCG may have been included in the 122 routes selected

 5         for the Application but may not have been included in the Applicants’ top 30 routes and

 6         likely would not have made the Top 6 routes. A copy of that Top 30 and Top 6 alternative

 7         route comparison is provided as my Exhibit JWD-CR1.


 8   Q.    BASED ON YOUR REVIEW OF MS. REINECKE’S DIRECT TESTIMONY, DO

 9         YOU AGREE WITH HER RECOMMENDATION THAT THE COMMISSION

10         ADOPT ROUTE CCG?

11   A.    No. Ms. Reinecke’s recommendation is premised on factors not included in the criteria the

12         Commission considers in selecting a route for a transmission line. In addition, her

13         recommendation mostly ignores three of the four more important routing factors.


14   Q.    PLEASE DESCRIBE THE TESTIMONY OF WITNESS THOMAS GHIDOSSI.

15   A.    Mr. Ghidossi provides testimony on behalf of the link G9 and link G13 landowners, who

16         are opposed to Route 894 and to any route that include links G9 and/or G13. His testimony

17         discusses concerns he has with the selection of links G9 and G13 and proposes that the

18         Commission consider additional routes north and south of links G9 and G13.


19   Q.    DOES MR. GHIDOSSI RECOMMEND ONE OF THE OTHER ALTERNATIVE

20         ROUTES?

21   A.    No.




     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                   Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                          9                         James W. Daniel
  1   Q.    DID MR. GHIDOSSI PROPOSE ADDITIONAL ROUTES NORTH AND SOUTH

 2         OF LINKS G9 AND G13 FOR THE COMMISSION TO CONSIDER?

 3   A.    No.


 4   Q.    DO YOU HAVE ANY COMMENTS ON MR. GHIDOSSI’S DIRECT TESTIMONY?

 5   A.    Yes. Mr. Ghidossi does not provide any analysis as to why the Commission should not

 6         approve Route 894. His issues are mostly concerns with the proposed line using links G9

 7         and G13.


 8                 III.    CONCERNS WITH FRAGMENTATION OF PROPERTIES


 9   Q.    IN YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY YOU ADDRESSED CONCERNS WITH

10         FRAGMENTATION             OF    A    LANDOWNER’S           PROPERTY.         DOES      MS.

11         REINECKE’S CCG ROUTE RESULT IN FRAGMENTATION OF PROPERTY?

12   A.    Yes. For example, on the Eastern side of the Study Area on Link F43, the proposed link

13         bisects Property ID Nos. 2579, 2577, 2561, and 2562 and as I noted in my direct testimony,

14         routes that include these links should not be approved as a route for the transmission line.

15         On the more westerly side of the Study area Link N4 splits properties noted as properties

16         identified as Property ID 480 And Property ID 481.


17   Q.    DID ANY INTERVENORS DISCUSS LINK N4 OR INCLUDE LINK N4 IN THEIR

18         RECOMMENDED ROUTES?

19   A.    Yes. Additionally, Ms. Reinecke’s proposed new alternative route CCG includes Link N4.




     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                     Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                          10                          James W. Daniel
  1   Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE PROBLEMS WITH ROUTES THAT INCLUDE LINK N4.

 2   A.      Based upon my review of the information provided in the EA regarding route N4 , some of

 3           the information appears to be incorrect.


 4   Q.      PLEASE EXPLAIN THE EA INFORMATION PROBLEM REGARDING LINK N4.

 5   A.      The problem relates to the length the Applicants claim is parallel to “apparent” property

 6           boundaries for routes that employ, e.g., Link N4. The database the Applicants use for

 7           identifying apparent property lines are electronic county tax appraisal maps of their

 8           property tax parcels1. This incorrectly assumes that property ownership boundaries and

 9           property tax parcel boundaries are identical. It is common for a landowner’s property to

10           include multiple contiguous property tax parcels. In that situation, the Applicants could

11           route a line along property tax parcel boundaries and claim it is parallel to “apparent”

12           property boundaries even though it is not on the property’s actual boundary. To illustrate

13           this problem, below is a diagram of a portion of the route for Link N4.




     1
      As stated on page 4-1 of the EA “The initial property boundary maps utilized to locate apparent property boundaries
     consisted of GIS data from the applicable county tax offices and appraisal districts.”

     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                                  Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                                    11                             James W. Daniel
  1                                         Routing of Link N4




 2


 3         As shown in the EA, Link N4 is shown as parallel with the boundary between Property ID

 4         480 and Property ID 481. Presumably, the Applicants have included the length of this

 5         portion of Link N4 in its statistics for “length of route parallel to apparent property

 6         boundaries” and “total length of route parallel to existing compatible rights-of-way”.

 7         However, based on property records, Property IDs 480 and 481 are shown as 2 property

 8         tax parcels, but are owned by the same landowner. The result is that the EA data would be

 9         overstating the length of the line that is parallel to property lines and parallel to existing

10         compatible ROWs. The effect is to make Link N4, and any route that includes Link N4,

11         look more favorable than it is. The extent of this problem along the rest of Link N4 (or

12         other links) is not known.




     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                      Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                           12                          James W. Daniel
  1   Q.    DO YOU HAVE ANY OTHER COMMENTS REGARDING FIGURE 1 ABOVE?

 2   A.    Yes. I previously discussed the problem of property fragmentation when a transmission

 3         line is routed through a previously undisturbed property as opposed to routing the line

 4         parallel to the property boundaries. The proposed route for Link N4 shown on Figure 1

 5         appears to not cause any property fragmentation. However, the portion of the Applicants’

 6         map shown in Figure 1 is misleading since the properties have a single ownership..


 7   Q.    WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION REGARDING LINK N4?

 8   A.    Based on the testimony of other intervenor witnesses and the issues discussed above, as

 9         with Links B3, F42 and F43, I do not believe the Commission should approve a route that

10         includes Link N4.


11                                      IV.     OTHER COMMENTS


12   Q.    DO YOU HAVE ANY OTHER COMMENTS REGARDING THE TESTIMONY

13         FILED BY OTHER INTERVENORS?

14   A.    Yes. I have two additional comments. One comment relates to the testimony of the Burnet

15         County Commissioners. The other comment relates to the very large number of individual

16         landowners that filed direct testimony.




     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                   Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                            13                      James W. Daniel
 1    Q.    PLEASE      DISCUSS       THE     TESTIMONY          OF    THE     BURNET        COUNTY

2          COMMISSIONERS.

3    A.    Several Burnet County Commissioners filed testimony in this case, including one that

4          addresses just the route adequacy issues. Generally, the Commissioners’ testimony opposes

5          all routes that “traverse” Burnet County. Since all the Applicants’ proposed 122 alternative

6          routes include links in Burnet County and SOAH Order No. 13 determined that the 122

 7         routes met the route adequacy threshold, avoiding impacts on Burnet County is not possible

 8         in this proceeding.


 9   Q.    PLEASE DISCUSS THE VERY LARGE NUMBER OF LANDOWNERS THAT

10         FILED DIRECT TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE.

11   A.    The eastern portion of the study area in this proceeding includes several cities and many

12         other developed areas. This has resulted in a very large number of interventions in the case

13         by homeowners and small landowners. A large portion of these landowners have also filed

14         direct testimony on their own behalf. Much of that testimony is discussing why the

15         intervenor does not want the transmission line to be on or near their property. There are

16         also many testimonies that appear to be standardized or coordinated. For example, there

17         are at least 39 witnesses that have filed testimony opposing the use of Link A2 since it

18         impacts their property. While I have not reviewed all of that A2-related testimony, the ones

19         that I have reviewed have the same testimony sections and format.


20         I understand why property owners do not want transmission lines on their property and that

21         they have standing to participate in this hearing. I just have two comments or concerns.

22         First, the number of witnesses opposing a route, including Route 894, should not be given

23         weight under the Commission’s routing criteria. Second, “not wanting the proposed line on

     SOAH Docket No.473-26-16349                                     Cross-Rebuttal Testimony of
     PUC Docket No. 59475                          14                          James W. Daniel
  1         their property” is not a differentiating factor in selecting a route that best meets the

 2         Commission’s routing criteria.


 3                                     V.      RECOMMENDATION


 4   Q.    BASED ON THE INTERVENOR TESTIMONY YOU REVIEWED, HAVE YOU

 5         CHANGED THE RECOMMENDATIONS IN YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY?

 6   A.    Only slightly, and that is in regard to Link N4 discussed above; the Commission should not

 7         site a transmission line on the new route CCG proposed by Ms. Reinecke.


 8   Q.    WOULD YOU PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATION?

 9   A.    My recommendation continues to be that the Commission            approve the Applicants’

10         proposed Route 894. In the event that the Commission does not approve Route 894, then I

11         recommend that routes that include Links B3, F42, F43 and N4 not be approved.


12   Q.    DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR CROSS-REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

13   A.    Yes, it does.
